toefl-reading.title: TOEFL Reading — Tips, Tricks & Strategy
toefl-reading.summary: Master academic reading comprehension: passage types, question styles, time management, and proven strategies to boost your score.

slides.title: What is TOEFL Reading?
points: Academic reading comprehension section of the TOEFL iBT exam
Tests your ability to understand English academic texts and lectures
Part of an integrated, four-skill test for international students
Widely accepted by universities, colleges, and institutions worldwide

slides.title: Reading Section Format & Timing
points: 3 passages, each 250–350 words long
10 questions per passage, 30 questions total
54 minutes total time (18 minutes per passage)
Question types: single-select, multiple-select, fill-in-a-table, insert-sentence

slides.title: TOEFL Reading Scoring
points: Scored out of 30 points (raw: 0–30)
Each correct answer = 1 point on average
Multiple-select and table-completion worth more (2–3 points each)
No penalty for incorrect answers; guess on time pressure

slides.title: Understanding Passage Types
points: Social sciences: history, anthropology, business, education topics
Natural sciences: biology, physics, chemistry, geology, environment
Humanities: art, music, literature, philosophy, culture
All passages are factual, neutral, academic in tone

slides.title: Main Idea & Purpose Questions
points: Identify the central idea or primary purpose of the passage
Read the first and last sentences carefully for main idea
Look for topic sentence in opening paragraphs
Eliminate answers that focus on minor details only
slides.tip: Main idea questions often use phrasing: 'The passage is mainly about' or 'The primary purpose of the passage is to'.
slides.warn: Do not confuse a supporting detail with the main idea. Reread the entire passage if unsure.

slides.title: Factual Information & Detail Questions
points: Answer based on explicit information in the passage
Look for specific facts: numbers, names, dates, findings
Use keywords from the question to locate the relevant paragraph
Paraphrase is common; answer may reword the passage text

example.label: Example
example.text: Q: According to the passage, when did the process begin? A: Find the paragraph mentioning time, match keywords like 'began', 'started', or 'in [year]'.

slides.warn: Watch for close but incorrect alternatives. The passage must directly support the answer.

slides.title: Inference Questions
points: Infer what the author implies but does not directly state
Use evidence from the passage to support your inference
Connect facts or statements that suggest a conclusion
Inference is logical, not a wild guess from background knowledge
slides.tip: Look for phrases: 'The passage implies', 'It can be inferred', 'suggests that'.
slides.warn: Inferences must be supported by the text. Do not use outside knowledge to answer.

slides.title: Vocabulary in Context Questions
points: Determine the meaning of a word as used in the passage
Read the surrounding sentences for clues (synonyms, definitions, examples)
Consider different word meanings; use context to narrow down
Often tested on academic or technical terms with multiple meanings

example.label: Example
example.text: Word 'critical' in 'The critical factor was timing' likely means 'important', not 'negative'. Use context clues.

slides.title: Reference & Pronoun Questions
points: Identify what a pronoun (he, she, it, they, this, that) refers to
Look backward in the text for the nearest appropriate noun
Ensure the pronoun agrees in number and context with the noun
Test your choice by substituting the noun for the pronoun
slides.tip: Pronouns usually refer to the most recently mentioned noun that matches in number (singular/plural).
slides.warn: Don't assume the nearest noun is always correct. Read for logical sense.

slides.title: Rhetorical Purpose Questions
points: Identify why the author included a specific sentence or example
Consider the function: support main idea, provide evidence, give contrast, illustrate
Reread the context before and after the referenced text
Questions often ask: 'Why does the author mention...?'
slides.tip: Examples are usually included to support or illustrate a point. Look for the claim being supported.

slides.title: Sentence Insertion (Insert Text) Questions
points: Choose the best location in the passage to insert a given sentence
Read the provided sentence and find the logical position
Check for pronoun reference and topic flow
Ensure the inserted sentence connects smoothly with surrounding text

example.label: Example
example.text: If inserting a sentence with 'However', it should contrast with the previous sentence. Check logical flow.

slides.warn: Smooth transition is key. Wrong placement breaks paragraph coherence and logic.

slides.title: Fill-in-a-Table (Summary) Questions
points: Select 3 or more correct answers from 6–7 options to complete a table or summary
Distinguish main ideas from supporting details
Some answers may be true but not directly support the passage's main points
The table often organizes ideas by category, comparison, or chronology
slides.tip: Look at the table structure first. It shows you what categories or relationships the passage covers.
slides.warn: Correct but irrelevant answers are included. Match answers to the table's purpose, not just accuracy.

slides.title: Multiple-Select Questions
points: Choose 2 or 3 correct answers from 4 options
All correct answers must be directly supported by the passage
One answer is typically plausible but incorrect or contradicted by text
Partial credit may apply (check test instructions)
slides.tip: Read each option against the passage. Multiple-correct questions reward precision.
slides.warn: Eliminate answers carefully. One wrong choice means zero points for that question on some tests.

slides.title: Time Management Strategy
points: Allocate 18 minutes per passage (54 minutes ÷ 3 passages)
Read the passage first (6–7 minutes), then answer questions (10–11 minutes)
Mark difficult questions and return if time permits
Spend more time on high-point questions (multiple-select, tables)
slides.tip: Skimming entire passage first helps you locate information faster when answering questions.

slides.title: Pre-Reading & Skimming Techniques
points: Read the first sentence of each paragraph (topic sentences)
Scan for paragraph structure: main claim followed by support
Notice transitions (however, therefore, similarly) that signal relationships
Identify the passage's overall organization before diving into questions
slides.tip: Active skimming takes 5–6 minutes and gives you a mental map of the passage, speeding up question-answering.

slides.title: Keyword Strategy for Locating Answers
points: Extract key words from each question before searching the passage
Look for the same words or synonyms in the passage
Use the find-and-replace feature (Ctrl+F) if testing on computer
Narrow your search to a specific paragraph; read it carefully

example.label: Example
example.text: Q: 'According to the passage, what caused the extinction?' Keywords: extinction, caused. Search passage for these terms.

slides.title: Effective Note-Taking During Reading
points: Write brief notes on the passage structure (intro, main points, conclusion)
Record paragraph topics next to paragraph numbers
Jot down key figures, dates, names as you encounter them
Use abbreviations and symbols (→ for 'caused', + for 'added', etc.)
slides.tip: Notes should take <2 minutes total and fit in margins. They're a safety net, not a complete summary.

slides.title: Top Reading Mistakes & Traps
points: Confusing main idea with a supporting detail
Using background knowledge instead of passage evidence
Misreading similar answer choices; read all options carefully
Running out of time due to slow reading or rereading entire passage
slides.warn: Many wrong answers are plausible. Eliminate based on passage support, not on what 'sounds right'.

slides.title: Common Distractor Patterns
points: Correct in general knowledge, but not stated in this passage
Opposite of the correct answer (tricky for inference questions)
Too narrow: mentions part of the idea, not the full picture
Too broad: general statement that doesn't match the passage's focus
slides.tip: When unsure, eliminate distractors first. Narrow the field before selecting an answer.

slides.title: Academic Vocabulary to Know
points: Common academic terms: hypothesis, theory, mechanism, facilitate, deteriorate, adapt, evolve
Transition words: moreover, conversely, subsequently, whereas, albeit
Comparison words: analogous, parallel, similar, divergent, distinct
Cause-effect: precipitate, consequence, attribute, stem from, yield
slides.tip: Learn word families: evolve, evolution, evolving. Academic texts repeat related terms.

slides.title: Worked Example: Science Passage
points: Passage: 'Photosynthesis is the process by which plants convert sunlight into chemical energy...'
Main idea Q: Answer focuses on the overall process, not just chlorophyll or glucose details.
Detail Q: 'According to the passage, what do plants use as an energy source?' Answer: sunlight (directly stated).
Inference Q: 'What can be inferred about plants in shade?' Answer: Logic from passage that light is essential.

example.label: Strategy
example.text: Locate key term in passage (photosynthesis) → Read around it → Match to question → Eliminate wrong answers.

slides.title: Worked Example: History Passage
points: Passage: 'The Renaissance began in Italy in the 14th century due to trade and wealth accumulation.'
Detail Q: 'When did the Renaissance begin?' Answer: 14th century (directly stated).
Inference Q: 'Why did the Renaissance likely start in Italy?' Answer: Trade and wealth accumulation (reasons given).
Multiple-select: Identify 3 factors that led to the Renaissance from passage evidence.
slides.tip: History passages often explain causes, effects, and sequences. Track timelines and causal chains.

slides.title: Pre-Test Checklist
points: Have you read academic articles or journals in the past month?
Can you quickly identify main ideas in unfamiliar texts?
Do you know 50+ high-frequency academic vocabulary words?
Can you complete a 18-minute passage with 10 questions in one sitting?
slides.tip: If any answer is no, spend 1–2 weeks on targeted practice before test day.

slides.title: Advanced: Scanning for Patterns
points: Problem-solution passages: introduction of problem, followed by proposed solutions, evaluation
Cause-effect passages: events are linked by causation; note the sequence
Comparison passages: two or more items contrasted; watch for 'however', 'unlike', 'differs'
Chronological passages: events ordered by time; track dates and 'before', 'after'
slides.tip: Recognizing passage structure helps you predict where the author is going and answer questions faster.

slides.title: Target Scores & Practice Plan
points: Beginner (0–19): Read 2–3 academic articles weekly, focus on main idea and basic detail questions
Intermediate (20–24): Practice all question types, time yourself, review errors daily
Advanced (25–30): Aim for 100% accuracy on detail and vocabulary, speed up to 15 minutes per passage
slides.tip: Use official TOEFL practice tests (ets.org). Official material is the best predictor of test performance.

slides.title: Reading on Computer vs. Paper
points: TOEFL iBT is delivered on computer; practice reading digitally
Use highlighter tool on screen to mark key sentences
No scrolling back to earlier passages; read each passage once and move on
Adapt to screen brightness and font size; practice in similar conditions
slides.warn: Screen fatigue is real. Practice in 54-minute blocks to build stamina for test day.

slides.title: Next: Practice & Mock Tests
points: Take full-length TOEFL reading simulations (54 minutes, 3 passages)
Review every wrong answer: why was it wrong, what did you miss?
Track your weak areas: main idea, inference, vocabulary, time management
Use Syllab's free TOEFL reading mock tests to build confidence and accuracy

example.label: Action
example.text: Complete 3 full mock tests this week. Spend 10 minutes reviewing errors after each test.

toefl-listening.title: TOEFL Listening — Tips, Tricks & Strategy
toefl-listening.summary: Master academic listening: conversation and lecture formats, question types, note-taking strategies, and proven techniques to maximize your score.

slides.title: What is TOEFL Listening?
points: Academic listening comprehension section of the TOEFL iBT exam
Tests your ability to understand English in academic and campus settings
Audio is played once; you cannot rewind or replay during the test
Uses realistic university dialogues and lectures with natural accents

slides.title: Listening Section Format & Timing
points: 3–4 conversations (3 minutes each) and 2–3 lectures (5–6 minutes each)
Each conversation has 5 questions; each lecture has 6 questions
Total: 28–34 questions in 41–56 minutes of actual listening plus answering
Questions appear on screen after each conversation or lecture

slides.title: TOEFL Listening Scoring
points: Scored out of 30 points (raw: 0–30)
Each question worth approximately 1 point
Multiple-select and replay-able sections worth slightly more
No penalty for incorrect answers; answer all questions before time expires

slides.title: Conversation Types & Topics
points: Student-professor office hours: course advice, assignment clarification, grade concerns
Student-staff interactions: registration, housing, financial aid, campus services
Settings: campus buildings, registrar's office, student center, dorm, library
Tone: friendly, informative, often with a problem or request for help

slides.title: Lecture Types & Topics
points: Science lectures: biology, chemistry, physics, environmental science, astronomy
Social science lectures: history, psychology, economics, anthropology, sociology
Humanities lectures: literature, philosophy, art history, music, cultural studies
Lectures include main ideas, supporting details, examples, and sometimes discussion

slides.title: Main Idea & Purpose Questions
points: Identify the primary topic or purpose of the conversation or lecture
Listen for what the speaker emphasizes or returns to repeatedly
Main idea is usually stated early; later details support it
Lectures often open with 'Today we'll discuss...' or 'The topic is...'

example.label: Example
example.text: Lecture: 'Today we're exploring photosynthesis. Photosynthesis is the process... Let me explain why it matters...' Main idea: What photosynthesis is and why it's important.

slides.tip: If you miss the opening, listen for repetition. The speaker will restate the main idea.

slides.title: Detail Questions
points: Answer based on specific information: facts, numbers, reasons, outcomes
Listen for supporting examples and explanations after the main point
Speaker may list details: 'First... Second... Finally...' or 'For example...'
Details are often harder to catch; good note-taking helps here
slides.tip: When you hear 'for instance' or 'in other words', the speaker is likely providing a detail or clarification.

slides.title: Inference Questions
points: Infer meaning from tone, emphasis, and what is NOT directly stated
Pay attention to the speaker's attitude: enthusiastic, skeptical, cautious, confident
Implied information from the context: 'The student didn't show up' implies absence or failure
Inference in listening relies heavily on speaker tone and emphasis
slides.tip: Listen to how things are said, not just what. Sarcasm, hesitation, and emphasis carry meaning.
slides.warn: Inferences are logical guesses based on audio cues, not assumptions from outside knowledge.

slides.title: Function Questions
points: Identify why the speaker said something: to clarify, give an example, change direction, summarize
Listen for: 'Let me explain', 'For instance', 'Actually', 'In conclusion', 'However'
Function questions ask: 'Why does the speaker mention...?' or 'What does the speaker mean by...?'
Common functions: explain, exemplify, contradict, summarize, persuade

example.label: Example
example.text: Speaker: 'That's one approach, but I think there's a better way...' Function: Introduce an alternative or contradict the previous point.

slides.title: Attitude & Tone Questions
points: Identify the speaker's attitude: positive, negative, neutral, surprised, skeptical
Listen for word choice: 'amazingly', 'unfortunately', 'interestingly'
Tone is conveyed through voice speed, pitch, and emphasis
A professor's hesitation or sarcasm reveals attitude toward a topic
slides.tip: When answers include emotional words (frustrated, fascinated, dismissive), listen for matching tone in audio.
slides.warn: The speaker's attitude toward one topic does not necessarily reflect attitude toward another.

slides.title: Sequence & Organization Questions
points: Understand the order of events, steps in a process, or flow of ideas
Listen for time markers: 'first', 'next', 'after that', 'finally', 'then'
Lectures often explain a process step-by-step or in chronological order
Conversations reveal sequence of what happened or what will happen

example.label: Example
example.text: Lecture: 'The water cycle has three main steps: evaporation, condensation, and precipitation. First, evaporation occurs...'

slides.title: Multiple-Select Questions
points: Choose 2 or 3 correct answers from 4–5 options
All correct answers must be supported by the audio
One plausible-sounding answer is typically wrong
Questions often ask: 'Which of the following are mentioned...?'
slides.tip: Listen for specific supporting points. Eliminate answers that were not mentioned or are contradicted.

slides.title: Note-Taking Strategy for Listening
points: Write short phrases, not full sentences (too slow)
Use abbreviations: Prof = professor, bio = biology, w/ = with, b/c = because
Symbol system: → (leads to), ↑ (increases), X (problem), ✓ (good point)
Organize by topic: main idea at top, details below, indented

example.label: Example
example.text: Note: 'Photosyn = plants convert light → chemical energy. Steps: 1) light reaction, 2) dark reaction.' Brief, scannable, complete.

slides.tip: Review your notes immediately after the audio ends. If something is unclear, jot a clarification.

slides.title: Active Listening Techniques
points: Predict: before each audio, read the questions if available and anticipate the topic
Engage: Mentally summarize main points as the speaker talks
Verify: Compare what you predict with what you hear
Recap: After the audio, write a one-sentence summary of the main idea
slides.tip: Active listening prevents mind-wandering. Engage your brain from sentence one.

slides.title: Handling Unfamiliar Accents & Speech Rates
points: TOEFL audio features diverse accents (British, Australian, North American, Indian)
Speakers vary pace and clarity; some are faster, some slower
Context clues help: if you miss a word, listen to surrounding words
Most TOEFL audio is clear; poor audio quality is not a major issue
slides.tip: Practice listening to diverse English accents outside the test (YouTube, podcasts, Ted Talks) to build ear adaptability.
slides.warn: Do not assume you misheard. Trust your ears and move forward; dwelling slows you down.

slides.title: Top Listening Mistakes & Traps
points: Daydreaming: mind wanders during a lecture; miss entire segments
Fixating on one word: getting stuck on an unknown word and losing the rest of the audio
Overwriting notes: trying to transcribe too much, hands cramping, missing content
Answering too fast: selecting an answer based on the first matching word, not full context
slides.warn: If you miss something, let it go. Focusing on what's past wastes energy on what's ahead.

slides.title: Common Distractor Patterns
points: Mentioned in audio but not relevant to the question asked
Opposite of what the speaker said (common for inference questions)
Partially correct: captures part of the idea but misses the full picture
Requires outside knowledge not in the audio (trap for educated guesses)
slides.tip: Eliminate answers that were not explicitly or implicitly stated in the audio.

slides.title: Academic Listening Vocabulary
points: Transition phrases: furthermore, in addition, on the other hand, as a result, in conclusion
Lecture markers: 'The key point is', 'This is important', 'Let me clarify', 'Don't forget that'
Expressions: 'Come to my office hours', 'Let me know by Friday', 'I'll send you the reading list'
Hedging language: 'I think', 'It seems', 'It could be', 'possibly', 'apparently'
slides.tip: Speakers use hedging when uncertain. Pay attention: certainty vs. speculation matters for inference.

slides.title: Worked Example: Conversation
points: Audio: Student asks professor about a missed class and upcoming exam.
Main idea Q: Student seeking guidance on makeup work and exam preparation.
Detail Q: 'What is the exam date?' Listen for the professor's specific response.
Function Q: 'Why does the student mention missing class?' To explain absence and request help.
Inference Q: 'What can you infer about the student's attitude?' Audio shows concern, diligence.

example.label: Note-taking
example.text: Student missed class. Exam next Fri. Prof says review Ch 5-7, come to office hours Thurs. Student seems worried but motivated.

slides.title: Worked Example: Lecture
points: Audio: Biology lecture on cellular respiration, phases, and energy production.
Main idea: Cells break down glucose to produce ATP (energy) in multiple stages.
Detail Q: 'What are the three main stages?' Glycolysis, Krebs cycle, electron transport chain.
Inference Q: 'Why does the professor emphasize ATP production?' Shows importance for cell function.
Multiple-select: Which statements about glycolysis are mentioned? (Identify correct answers from audio.)
slides.tip: Science lectures often explain process. Draw diagrams or flow charts in your notes to track steps.

slides.title: Pre-Test Listening Habits
points: Listen to English podcasts, documentaries, or lectures 3–5 times weekly
Watch English movies or videos with subtitles, then without
Attend live university lectures or TED Talks to adjust to pacing and accent
Practice note-taking while listening to academic content
slides.tip: Consistent exposure builds listening stamina. Test day should not be your first time hearing academic lectures.

slides.title: Target Scores & Practice Plan
points: Beginner (0–19): Listen to 2–3 short conversations daily, focus on main idea
Intermediate (20–24): Practice full conversations and lectures, refine note-taking, review errors
Advanced (25–30): Aim for 100% accuracy on detail, function, and inference questions; speed up note-taking
slides.tip: Official TOEFL listening practice materials (ets.org) are the most accurate representation of test audio.

slides.title: Using Keyboard Shortcuts During Test
points: Pause button: Use only if you finish notes early and need to mentally prepare for questions
Play button: Some questions allow replaying portions of audio; use strategically
Volume: Adjust at the very beginning; poor audio should be reported to proctor
Headphones: Ensure fit is comfortable before audio begins; do not adjust once playing
slides.warn: Wasting time adjusting settings costs you answering time. Get comfortable before the audio starts.

slides.title: Next: Practice & Mock Tests
points: Complete full-length TOEFL listening simulations (3–4 conversations, 2–3 lectures)
Review each question: Did you understand the question? Did you hear the answer?
Track weak areas: specific question types, certain speakers, fast speech
Use Syllab's free TOEFL listening mock tests with real audio and question formats

example.label: Action
example.text: Take 3 full listening mocks this week. After each, identify 2 questions you got wrong and understand why.

toefl-speaking.title: TOEFL Speaking — Tips, Tricks & Strategy
toefl-speaking.summary: Master academic speaking: task formats, integrated and independent tasks, preparation tips, delivery strategies, and scoring rubrics to maximize your score.

slides.title: What is TOEFL Speaking?
points: Academic speaking section tests your ability to speak English clearly and coherently
You speak into a microphone; responses are recorded and later scored
Includes independent speaking (your own ideas) and integrated speaking (reading + listening + speaking)
Designed to measure university-level communication skills

slides.title: Speaking Section Format & Timing
points: 4 tasks total: 1 independent (Task 1), 3 integrated (Tasks 2–4)
Task 1: 15 seconds prep, 45 seconds response (independent opinion)
Tasks 2–3: 30 seconds prep, 60 seconds response (read passage, listen, speak)
Task 4: 20 seconds prep, 60 seconds response (listen, speak without reading)
Total: 16 minutes (3 minutes speaking + 13 minutes prep/reading/listening)

slides.title: TOEFL Speaking Scoring
points: Scored out of 30 points (each task weighted equally at 0–30)
Rubric evaluates: delivery (clarity, pace, pronunciation), language use (grammar, vocabulary), topic development (completeness, coherence)
Raters listen for natural, fluent speech; near-native pronunciation not required
Common score range: 18–26 for strong test-takers

slides.title: Task 1: Independent Speaking
points: You are asked for your personal opinion on a topic (e.g., 'Describe a memorable experience')
15 seconds to prepare; 45 seconds to speak
No reading or listening required; draw from your own experience and ideas
Goal: Share a clear opinion with 2–3 relevant details or examples

example.label: Example Topic
example.text: Describe a hobby or interest you enjoy. Why do you find it rewarding? Use specific details in your explanation.

slides.tip: Use the prep time to plan: main idea (45 seconds = roughly 110–130 words), 2 supporting points, brief conclusion.

slides.title: Task 1: Strategies & Template
points: Template: Introduction (topic + main reason) → Detail 1 (explain + example) → Detail 2 (explain + example) → Conclusion (restate reason)
Keep introduction short (15 seconds of your 45-second response) to leave time for details
Use connectors: 'First of all', 'Specifically', 'Another reason is', 'In conclusion'
Sound conversational; avoid sounding robotic or overly scripted
slides.tip: Personal examples are stronger than abstract statements. Use 'I' and specific details.
slides.warn: Pausing to think is okay; awkward silence is not. Speak smoothly and confidently.

slides.title: Task 2: Integrated Speaking (Read-Listen-Speak)
points: Read a short passage (75–100 words) about a campus announcement, policy, or academic topic
Listen to a conversation (60–90 seconds) between a student and professor/staff responding to the announcement
45 seconds to speak: summarize the conversation and the speaker's opinion
You must include both the announcement and the student's personal perspective

slides.title: Task 2: Strategies & Template
points: During reading: Note the announcement key points (what changed, when, why)
During listening: Focus on the student's opinion and reasons (agrees, disagrees, concerned, excited)
Template: Announcement (the change) → Student's opinion (agree/disagree) → Reason 1 → Reason 2 → Conclusion
Balance: Give equal time to announcement and student's view

example.label: Example
example.text: Announcement: Library hours extended. Student says: Great! Can study late. Prefers quiet at night. Easier to find resources after class.

slides.tip: The student's opinion is the focus. Announcement is context. Lead with what the student thinks.

slides.title: Task 3: Integrated Speaking (Read-Listen-Speak, Lecture)
points: Read a short academic passage (75–100 words) introducing a concept or theory
Listen to a lecture excerpt (90–120 seconds) expanding on the concept with examples
60 seconds to speak: explain the concept and how the lecture example illustrates it
Focus is academic understanding, not personal opinion

slides.title: Task 3: Strategies & Template
points: During reading: Identify the main concept or theory name, definition, key characteristics
During lecture: Listen for the professor's explanation and specific examples that clarify the concept
Template: Concept definition → Key characteristic or feature → Professor's example → How example illustrates concept → Conclusion
Use academic language: 'The lecture illustrates', 'This concept is demonstrated by', 'The professor explains'

example.label: Example
example.text: Concept: Operant conditioning (behavior shaped by consequences). Lecture: Examples of reinforcement (rewards) in animal training. Student explains how rewards reinforce behavior.

slides.tip: Show you understand the concept. The example should clearly connect to the theory.

slides.title: Task 4: Integrated Speaking (Listen-Speak, No Reading)
points: Listen to a lecture excerpt (90–120 seconds) on an academic topic
No reading; you take notes during listening
60 seconds to speak: summarize the main idea and supporting details from the lecture
Pure listening comprehension and summarization; no personal opinion

slides.title: Task 4: Strategies & Note-Taking
points: Listen for: Main topic (what the lecture is about), key points or themes, examples or evidence
Use symbols and abbreviations: → (leads to), ↑ (increases), ex. (example), w/ (with)
Template: Main idea → Key point 1 (with supporting detail) → Key point 2 (with supporting detail) → Conclusion
Speak from your notes; you do not need to memorize the lecture word-for-word

example.label: Example
example.text: Lecture: Evolution through natural selection. Fittest organisms survive. Ex: Peppered moths (dark moths survived industrial England). Notes: Nat. sel. → fittest survive; ex. peppered moths.

slides.tip: Structure your summary clearly. Listeners should follow your organization, not the lecture's complexity.

slides.title: Delivery: Pronunciation & Clarity
points: Speak clearly: Distinct consonants, steady pace (not too fast, not too slow)
Intonation: Vary pitch to emphasize key words and avoid monotone delivery
Confidence: Project your voice; speak as if addressing a classroom, not muttering
Accent: Near-native pronunciation is not required. Clear, intelligible English is the goal
slides.tip: Practice speaking aloud, not in your head. Record yourself and listen. Identify unclear words.
slides.warn: Speaking too fast under nervousness is a common trap. Pause for breath and emphasis.

slides.title: Language Use: Grammar & Vocabulary
points: Use complex sentences: 'Although X, Y because Z.' Show range of structures.
Vocabulary: Academic and topic-specific words when appropriate (not slang)
Fluency: Smooth transitions between ideas; avoid long pauses or filler words ('um', 'like')
Accuracy: Grammatical errors are okay if they do not impede understanding
slides.tip: Varied sentence structures show language control. Mix simple and complex sentences naturally.
slides.warn: Filler words and long pauses are marked down. Practice speaking without them.

slides.title: Topic Development: Completeness & Coherence
points: Directly answer the question or prompt
Provide 2–3 supporting details or reasons (Tasks 1–2) or key points from lecture (Tasks 3–4)
Explain how details support your main idea; do not just list facts
Conclude by restating your main point or summarizing the concept

example.label: Strong Response
example.text: Main idea stated → Detail 1 explained → Detail 2 explained → Conclusion. Each part connected by transitions.

slides.warn: Incomplete responses (missing details, no conclusion) score lower. Budget your 45–60 seconds wisely.

slides.title: Top Speaking Mistakes & Traps
points: Running out of time: Spending too long on the opening, rushing details, missing conclusion
Off-topic: Not directly answering the question; rambling to fill time
Unclear speech: Speaking too fast, mumbling, inconsistent volume
Poor organization: Ideas scattered, no clear structure, difficult to follow
slides.warn: Raters expect clear, organized responses. Practice structure as much as vocabulary.

slides.title: Common Scoring Traps
points: Accent is NOT scored; intelligibility is. Slight accents are fine.
Small grammar errors are forgivable; major errors that confuse meaning are not
Memorized responses sound unnatural and score lower than extemporaneous speech
Reading directly from notes scores lower than using notes as a guide and speaking naturally
slides.tip: Practice extemporaneous speaking (speaking on the spot with brief prep). That's what the test measures.

slides.title: Note-Taking for Integrated Tasks
points: Task 2 (read passage): Jot announcement key points in 15 seconds (e.g., 'Library hours: 8am–midnight')
Task 3 (read passage): Write concept name and 1–2 defining features (e.g., 'Operant conditioning: behavior shaped by consequences')
Task 4 (lecture only): Organize notes by main point and supporting details
Use legible writing and abbreviations. You'll have <30 seconds to review before speaking.
slides.tip: Your notes are for your reference, not to be read word-for-word. Use them as bullet points, not a script.

slides.title: Time Management During Speaking Section
points: Task 1: Spend 10 seconds planning, 35 seconds speaking (leave 5 seconds buffer)
Tasks 2–3: Spend 20 seconds reviewing notes, 40 seconds speaking (leave 5 seconds)
Task 4: Spend 15 seconds reviewing notes, 45 seconds speaking (leave 5 seconds)
Do not waste remaining time after you finish speaking; the recording auto-stops
slides.tip: During prep, write just enough to trigger your memory. Over-detailed notes waste time during delivery.

slides.title: Academic Speaking Vocabulary
points: Discourse markers: Furthermore, As a result, In contrast, To summarize, Therefore
Academic phrases: 'The main point is', 'This illustrates', 'One key aspect', 'In conclusion'
Linking ideas: 'Not only X but also Y', 'Both X and Y', 'X, whereas Y', 'X is similar to Y'
Subject-specific terms: vary by discipline (biology, history, business, psychology)
slides.tip: Academic language boosts scores. Practice using phrases like 'This example demonstrates' instead of 'This shows'.

slides.title: Worked Example: Task 1 (Independent)
points: Prompt: 'Describe an important goal you have. Why is this goal important to you?'
Prep plan: Choose goal (studying abroad) → Why (adventure, education) → Details (new skills, independence)
Response: Intro (goal is study abroad) → Detail 1 (learn new culture) → Detail 2 (develop independence) → Conclusion (growth matters)
Delivery: Speak clearly, vary pace, use transitions. Aim for ~110 words in 45 seconds.

example.label: Sample Response
example.text: My important goal is to study abroad. This is important because I want to experience a new culture and become more independent. First, I'll learn a different perspective on education... Second, living alone will help me... In conclusion, this goal will help me grow...

slides.title: Worked Example: Task 2 (Integrated)
points: Announcement: Dining hall changing hours (now open until midnight instead of 10pm)
Conversation: Student says great because late-night studying and can eat after events
Response structure: Announcement (hours extended) → Student opinion (positive) → Reason 1 (study late) → Reason 2 (eat late) → Conclusion
Delivery: Balance announcement and student perspective. Use connectors like 'The student thinks this is good because'.
slides.tip: Task 2 is about the student's opinion first, announcement context second. Lead with the student.

slides.title: Pre-Test Speaking Habits
points: Practice speaking aloud daily: Read news aloud, summarize videos, record yourself
Join conversation groups or language exchanges to practice extemporaneous speaking
Record your responses and listen critically: clarity, pace, organization, grammar
Simulate test conditions: 15–45 seconds prep, 45–60 seconds response, no revisions
slides.tip: Silent practice (thinking through responses) does NOT prepare you for speaking. Speak out loud, always.

slides.title: Target Scores & Practice Plan
points: Beginner (0–19): Practice Task 1 daily, focus on clarity and basic organization
Intermediate (20–24): Add integrated tasks (2–4), work on fluency and detail
Advanced (25–30): Aim for natural delivery, complex structures, detailed examples; practice all task types
slides.tip: Official TOEFL speaking practice with sample responses (ets.org) shows what high scores sound like.

slides.title: Next: Practice & Mock Tests
points: Complete full-length speaking simulations: Task 1 (independent), Tasks 2–4 (integrated)
Record and self-evaluate: Is it clear? Organized? Detailed? Do I answer the prompt?
Compare your response to sample high-scoring responses. Note differences.
Use Syllab's free TOEFL speaking mock tests for realistic practice and feedback

example.label: Action
example.text: This week, record 3 full speaking tests. Listen to your recordings and identify 2 areas to improve for next week.

toefl-writing.title: TOEFL Writing — Tips, Tricks & Strategy
toefl-writing.summary: Master academic writing: integrated essay and discussion task, essay structure, grammar, time management, and proven strategies to achieve higher scores.

slides.title: What is TOEFL Writing?
points: Academic writing section tests your ability to write clear, coherent English essays
2 tasks: 1 integrated (reading, listening, writing) and 1 independent (discussion/opinion)
Focuses on organizing ideas, supporting claims, and using accurate grammar
Essays are scored by human raters using a detailed rubric

slides.title: Writing Section Format & Timing
points: Task 1 (Integrated): Read passage (3 min) → listen to lecture (2 min) → write 150–225 words (20 min)
Task 2 (Academic Discussion): Read discussion prompt and posts (3 min) → write 100–150 words (10 min)
Total writing time: 30 minutes (20 minutes integrated, 10 minutes discussion)
No word count penalty for exceeding limits; quality is assessed regardless of length

slides.title: TOEFL Writing Scoring
points: Each task scored 0–5; total writing score = 0–30 (weighted combination)
Rubric evaluates: task completion (answering the prompt), organization, language (vocabulary, grammar), development (supporting details)
Common scores: 22–26 for strong test-takers; 26–30 is advanced
Coherence and clear argument are prioritized over perfect grammar

slides.title: Task 1: Integrated Writing (Read-Listen-Write)
points: Read a short academic passage (250–300 words) on a topic
Listen to a 2–3 minute lecture that CONTRADICTS or COMPLICATES the passage
Write 150–225 words summarizing the lecture's main points and how they relate to the reading
You are NOT stating your own opinion; you are reporting what the lecture says

slides.title: Task 1: Reading Strategy
points: Identify the passage's main argument or claim in the first 2 paragraphs
Note 2–3 supporting points from the passage (examples, evidence, explanation)
Expect the lecture to challenge, refute, or modify one or more of these points
Key question: What is the passage saying, and how will the lecture respond?

example.label: Example
example.text: Passage: 'Traditional zoos protect endangered species through breeding programs.' Lecture likely: Challenges effectiveness, discusses wild conservation instead, or questions welfare concerns.

slides.title: Task 1: Listening & Note-Taking
points: Focus on how the lecture contradicts, expands, or refines the passage
Note the professor's main point and 2–3 supporting reasons or examples
Use abbreviations: Prof = professor, trad = traditional, ex = example, w/ = with
Structure notes: Main claim → Supporting point 1 → Supporting point 2
slides.tip: The lecture's job is to complicate the reading. Expect a 'But' or 'However' tone. Identify what the lecture argues INSTEAD.
slides.warn: Do not mix up the passage's claim with the lecture's claim. Your essay reports both, showing the relationship.

slides.title: Task 1: Essay Template
points: Intro: Passage claims X (one sentence). Lecture challenges/expands this by stating Y (one sentence).
Paragraph 1: Passage point A + Lecture response to A (with evidence)
Paragraph 2: Passage point B + Lecture response to B (with evidence)
Conclusion: Restate how lecture complicates/modifies passage's argument

example.label: Structure
example.text: Para 1: Passage says zoos breed endangered animals. Lecture: Breeding often fails in wild; zoos cause stress. Para 2: Passage: zoos educate. Lecture: Visitors learn misconceptions. Conclusion: Lecture questions zoos' effectiveness.

slides.title: Task 1: Sample Integrated Essay
points: Intro: The reading suggests zoos protect species. The lecture argues zoos may harm conservation and animal welfare.
Para 1: Reading: zoos breed endangered species. Lecture: Species bred in zoos often cannot survive in wild. Programs often fail.
Para 2: Reading: zoos educate visitors about wildlife. Lecture: Visitors see confined animals, learning incorrect behaviors. Education is misguided.
Conclusion: While reading supports zoos, lecture demonstrates limitations in conservation and education.
slides.tip: Show clear relationships between passage and lecture. Use phrases: 'The lecture contradicts this by', 'This supports the claim', 'However, the lecture notes'.

slides.title: Task 2: Academic Discussion Task
points: Read a discussion prompt and 1–2 sample student posts on a topic
Write 100–150 words making an argument related to the discussion
You respond to the prompt, NOT to the student posts. Do not argue directly with other students.
Provide one clear claim with supporting evidence or reasoning

slides.title: Task 2: Understanding the Prompt
points: Prompt typically asks: 'Do you agree or disagree?' or 'Which perspective is stronger?'
Example: 'Should universities require in-person attendance? Why or why not?'
Student posts might argue for or against; you take a position, not summarize both
Your response adds a new perspective or reinforces an existing one with new evidence
slides.tip: Read the prompt carefully. Some ask for agreement, others ask for comparison. Answer the exact question asked.
slides.warn: Do not simply agree with one post. Develop your own argument supported by reasoning.

slides.title: Task 2: Essay Template
points: Intro: State your position clearly (agree/disagree or preference) in 1 sentence
Body: Provide 1–2 reasons with explanation or example. Keep it concise (100–150 words total).
Conclusion: Restate your position briefly and summarize why

example.label: Example Response
example.text: I believe universities should require in-person attendance because face-to-face interaction improves learning. Students engage in discussions, ask questions, and receive immediate feedback. Additionally, campus community building fosters collaboration. In conclusion, despite flexibility online offers, in-person attendance strengthens education.

slides.title: Organization & Clarity
points: Use clear paragraph breaks: introduction, body paragraphs, conclusion
Topic sentences start each paragraph and signal the main idea
Transition words connect ideas: Furthermore, However, As a result, For example
Conclusion summarizes main argument; avoid introducing new information
slides.tip: Organize ideas logically. A reader should follow your argument effortlessly from start to finish.

slides.title: Grammar & Vocabulary
points: Use varied sentence structures: simple, compound, complex sentences
Academic vocabulary: utilize, significant, contribute, demonstrate, substantial, relevant
Avoid repetition: vary word choice; use pronouns (this, that) to refer back
Check grammar: subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, apostrophes in contractions
slides.tip: Accuracy matters more than complexity. Clear, correct sentences score higher than fancy but awkward phrasing.
slides.warn: Grammatical errors do not automatically lower scores if overall meaning is clear. However, repeated errors hurt.

slides.title: Development & Support
points: Task 1: Report the lecture's points with specific evidence (direct quotes, paraphrases)
Task 2: Support your claim with reasons, examples, or explanations
Avoid unsupported assertions. Every main idea needs supporting detail.
Use your time to develop 1–2 strong points rather than listing 5 weak ideas

example.label: Weak vs. Strong
example.text: Weak: 'In-person attendance is important.' Strong: 'In-person attendance improves learning because students interact directly with professors, asking clarifying questions in real-time.'

slides.title: Time Management for Task 1
points: 0–3 min: Read the passage, identify main claim and 2 supporting points
3–5 min: Listen and take notes on how lecture challenges/complicates passage
5–7 min: Plan essay outline (intro, 2 body paragraphs, conclusion)
7–25 min: Write essay (150–225 words = roughly 20 minutes of typing)
25–27 min: Review for grammar and clarity
slides.tip: Plan your essay before typing. A clear outline saves time and improves coherence.

slides.title: Time Management for Task 2
points: 0–2 min: Read prompt and student posts, identify the exact question
2–3 min: Decide your position and plan 1–2 supporting points
3–9 min: Write essay (100–150 words = roughly 6 minutes of typing)
9–10 min: Proofread and fix obvious errors
slides.tip: Task 2 is short. Keep it tight. One strong argument beats multiple weak ones.

slides.title: Top Writing Mistakes & Traps
points: Task 1: Mixing passage and lecture claims; unclear which argument belongs where
Task 1: Adding your own opinion (prompt asks only for reporting, not analysis)
Task 2: Not answering the prompt; rambling on related topics instead
Both: Running out of time due to poor planning; incomplete essays
Both: Over-writing. More words do not equal higher scores; clarity and development do
slides.warn: Incomplete essays (missing conclusion, underdeveloped body) score significantly lower. Plan time to finish.

slides.title: Common Scoring Traps
points: Task 1: Summarizing the lecture but not connecting it to the passage = lower score
Task 1: Stating your opinion on the topic instead of reporting the lecture = off-task penalty
Task 2: Listing ideas without supporting reasons = underdeveloped
Both: Grammatically correct but incomprehensible organization = lower score for development
slides.tip: Re-read the prompt before writing. 'Report the lecture' ≠ 'Argue your opinion.' Know which you're doing.

slides.title: Proofreading Checklist
points: Did I answer the prompt fully (Task 1: report lecture + passage; Task 2: take a position)?
Does each paragraph have a clear topic sentence?
Are ideas connected with transition words?
Are sentences grammatically correct? (Subject-verb agreement, tense, punctuation)
Did I include supporting details or examples?
Is my conclusion present and meaningful (not just restating the intro)?
slides.tip: Set a 2-minute timer for proofreading. Fix obvious errors; do not rewrite entire paragraphs.

slides.title: Academic Writing Vocabulary
points: Transition phrases: Furthermore, However, On the other hand, As a result, In contrast, Additionally
Reporting verbs: The lecture argues, The author contends, The passage suggests, Research demonstrates
Qualifying language: suggests, may, appears, indicates (not absolute claims)
Academic nouns: evidence, benefit, drawback, consequence, contribution, limitation
slides.tip: Academic vocabulary elevates your writing. Use 'utilize' instead of 'use', 'significant' instead of 'big'.

slides.title: Worked Example: Task 1 Full Essay
points: Passage: Electric vehicles reduce emissions and combat climate change.
Lecture: Manufacturing batteries causes pollution; electricity from coal negates benefits.
Intro: Passage argues EVs reduce emissions. Lecture questions the net environmental benefit.
Para 1: Passage: EVs emit zero tailpipe. Lecture: Electricity production from coal generates emissions elsewhere.
Para 2: Passage: EVs reduce climate impact. Lecture: Battery manufacturing pollutes; recycling is limited.
Conclusion: Lecture complicates passage by shifting focus from use-phase to production-phase emissions.

example.label: Sample Essay (150+ words)
example.text: The reading claims electric vehicles reduce emissions and combat climate change. However, the lecture complicates this argument by highlighting hidden environmental costs. The passage suggests EVs produce zero tailpipe emissions, making them cleaner than gasoline cars. But the lecture notes that electricity generation often relies on coal power, meaning EVs simply shift emissions from tailpipes to power plants. Additionally, the reading emphasizes climate benefits, while the lecture argues battery manufacturing causes substantial pollution, and recycling infrastructure remains underdeveloped. In conclusion, while the passage presents a straightforward environmental argument for EVs, the lecture demonstrates that full lifecycle impacts are more complicated and potentially less beneficial than commonly believed.

slides.title: Worked Example: Task 2 Discussion Response
points: Prompt: 'Should universities prioritize teaching job skills or liberal arts education?'
Student 1: Job skills are essential for employment.
Student 2: Liberal arts develop critical thinking.
Your position: Argue for one, or propose a balance.
Response: Develop 1–2 reasons with explanation, then conclude

example.label: Sample Response (100–150 words)
example.text: While job skills are important, I believe universities should prioritize liberal arts education because critical thinking applies across all careers. Students who understand history, literature, and philosophy can analyze complex problems creatively, adapting to changing job markets. Job training becomes obsolete quickly, but skills like writing and reasoning remain valuable throughout life. Additionally, liberal arts education encourages informed citizenship, helping graduates contribute to society beyond their profession. In conclusion, universities serve students best by emphasizing liberal arts, which provides foundational skills that support both career success and meaningful citizenship.

slides.title: Pre-Test Writing Habits
points: Write daily: journal, summaries, opinion essays on topics you care about
Read academic articles and note structure: intro claim, supporting points, conclusion
Practice integrated essays: read + listen + write on similar formats to Task 1
Get feedback: exchange essays with peers or tutors; identify recurring errors
slides.tip: Consistent writing practice builds fluency and accuracy. Practice is the best teacher.

slides.title: Target Scores & Practice Plan
points: Beginner (0–19): Write 5 Task 1 essays weekly, focus on clear organization and grammar
Intermediate (20–24): Add Task 2 essays, practice time limits, refine vocabulary
Advanced (25–30): Aim for sophisticated arguments, minimal errors, strong development; practice all formats
slides.tip: Official TOEFL writing sample essays (ets.org) show what different score levels look like.

slides.title: Next: Practice & Mock Tests
points: Complete full-length writing simulations: Task 1 (integrated, 20 min) + Task 2 (discussion, 10 min)
After each essay, review: Did I answer the prompt? Is it organized? Are ideas developed?
Compare your essay to sample high-scoring responses from ETS
Use Syllab's free TOEFL writing mock tests for realistic practice and feedback

example.label: Action
example.text: This week, write 3 full integrated essays and 3 discussion responses. Proofread carefully, then review against sample essays to identify gaps.
